Messages.Author: jcrossn...@gmail.com
Messages.Body:
LSJ wrote:
> Hmm.
>
> I get the impression Lasombra was asking for game-legal tactical errors. May
> want to branch two topics for this (game-legal tactical errors players make, and
> rules that players forget/break).

Yeah, I was noticing that too as I read down the thread. Pointing out
that we should all remember to do stuff that is obviously either good
or required isn't all that interesting. Here are some common play
mistakes I see:

1. "Spooging" cards. This is when you play a card that you're likely
to need in the future at a time when it is far less helpful than it
could have been. For example, if you need to +2 stealth to succeed in
an action, and your only source of stealth is a Faceless Night, don't
play it hoping to draw another stealth card. The most likely result is
that you won't draw one, you'll still get blocked, and now you're down
a stealth card that you obviously needed.

2. Cycling for no reason. This is somewhat related, but a little
different. I often see people play as though the object of the game is
to run out of cards as fast as possible, or watch people do absurdly
stupid things just to draw new cards. The worst is when people cycle
like maniacs in the hopes of seeing something good, but have no clear
idea what it is they're looking for.

3. Spending counters you can't afford to spend. This often accompanies
the previous 2. You play a card with a cost on it just to get it out
of your hand, even though you can't afford the cost. This is probably
best solved at the deck construction level, where it's generally
better to avoid blood and pool costs except on cards that are vital to
your strategy.

I'm sure I could come up with more, but I have to go a different
thing.
Jesse

Messages.Author: Chris Berger
Messages.Body:
On May 26, 12:44 pm, jcrossnicker...@gmail.com wrote:
>
> 2. Cycling for no reason. This is somewhat related, but a little
> different. I often see people play as though the object of the game is
> to run out of cards as fast as possible, or watch people do absurdly
> stupid things just to draw new cards. The worst is when people cycle
> like maniacs in the hopes of seeing something good, but have no clear
> idea what it is they're looking for.
>

Something I see a lot more of than this is almost the opposite - not
discarding during your discard phase. Unless your hand is set up
perfectly for what you want to do, you should almost always discard.
I make it a rule to discard anything I can't use in the next 2 turns
(with a few exceptions, like Week of Nightmares or Archon
Investigation), to always discard a master card if I have more than 2
(not counting trifles), and to always discard an action card if I have
more of them in hand than I can play next turn (again, with some
exceptions). Two copies of the same reaction or action modifier?
Discard 1 if there's nothing better to ditch.

No matter how much you really want to hold onto that Far Mastery that
might have a use several turns down the line, or that Deflection when
you have no vamps with dominate but are hoping you might draw one from
your crypt or draw a skill card... no matter how much you love what's
in your hand for whatever reason, you could almost *always* have a
better hand. And you only get one free no-requirements no-strings-
attached chance to cycle each turn, so use it... I get almost
physically ill when I see someone sit there transferring the first 3
turns without discarding anything, and then I hear them complain that
they don't have the card they need once their giant minion can finally
act, or that they "just didn't draw any bounce". You skipped 3
potential chances to draw better cards!

Forgetting "Do Not Replace" and "Untap this" are procedural errors. They violate
the rules of the game (where rules of the game includes "follow card text").

Untapping via the Leather Jacket is not optional. It cannot be overlooked.
"Forgetting Leather Jacket" typically means this.

"Forgetting that the Leather Jacket effect will untap a given minion later this
turn", well, that's something else, yes (see below).

> Or: I
> thought I could oust my prey but had forgotten that one minion already
> had bled this turn. Now I�m all but tapped out...

Ah, misremembering game history (like "VampireBob will untap this turn because
of the Leather Jacket"), a third type of error. This type can easily be argued
to be a type of tactical error of the kind Lasombra gave examples.

> Do not replace, however, that�s rulebreaking. I don�t know if that�s
> an "in-game mistake". My english isn�t good enough!

It's a violation of the rules (like not untapping via the "untap this" effect
from Leather Jacket is), different than the types of tactical errors (or a
broader term to encompass game history and the like: game-legal oversights)
given by Lasombra.

Messages.Author: LSJ
Messages.Body:
brandons...@yahoo.com wrote:
> LSJ, in the case of violating the DNR rule on a card or just plain
> over-drawing, what would you say the best remedy is?
>
> -place the card back on top of your library
> -place the card in your library and shuffle
> -show the card to other players, then shuffle it into your library
> -all/some of the above
> -other

If no one had seen the card prior to it being mis-drawn (and the library is
otherwise "random" to all concerned), then put it back and shuffle.

If the card had already been known to some party, then find appropriate response
(if the only person who had seen the card prior to the mis-draw was the player
who drew it, then putting it back on top is perfect).

Other players who hadn't seen the card would have no reason to see it just for
it being mis-drawn.

> I would think that an apology would be appropriate, in addition to
> other solutions.

Always apologize when you break a rule, sure.

put the card back on top.

Messages.Author: LSJ
Messages.Body:

Um. No. The general rule, as above, is to make a random draw random again by
shuffling.

You only "put it back on top and don't reshuffle" if someone (you or someone
else) had already seen the card and knew it was on top of your deck (and doing
so wouldn't give you an improper advantage).

That's being consistent.
